in_text_mentions: Described by Cogan in 1964, EBMD is characterized by bilateral, and frequently asymmetric, subepithelial fingerprint lines, geographic maps, and epithelial microcysts or dots and bleb patterns shown by slit-lamp examination [3, 4] (Fig 1). Histopathology reveals an abnormal basement membrane that protrudes into the epithelium and the presence of intraepithelial pseudocysts and layers of accumulated intraepithelial material [5, 6].

The extent to which COD can be used to differentiate EBMD from other ocular surface diseases remains to be elucidated. As shown in Fig. 1, the Pentacam’s color-coded densitometry may reveal characteristic surface alterations even in the absence of the patient. While the characteristic corneal changes of EBMD can be effectively visualized and mapped using COD, facilitating its differentiation from other ocular surface conditions (e.g., dry eye disease, keratopathy, guttate cornea), it may be challenging to define a specific numerical threshold for clinical application. B: Anterior segment OCT of the patient's right eye showing a basement membrane abnormality and hyperreflective epithelial region characteristic of EBMD; captioned manifestations do not exactly match vocabulary keys, so they are proposed_findings. C: Anterior segment OCT of the patient's left eye with diffuse epithelial basement membrane thickening, a hallmark EBMD finding; vocabulary lacks an OCT-specific basement-membrane thickening key, so findings are proposed. D: Slit-lamp photograph of the patient's left cornea with textbook geographic map-like lines surrounding epithelial dots - classic map-dot-fingerprint EBMD presentation.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: In vivo confocal microscopy of an EBMD patient's basal epithelium showing hyperreflective extracellular deposits corresponding to map-like/map-line changes described in the caption and text. B: Confocal image of basal epithelium with hyporeflective/curvilinear line pattern explicitly matched to the fingerprint lines of EBMD in caption and text. C: Linear and ring-shaped hyperreflective material at the epithelial basement membrane in an EBMD patient, matching the geographic/map-line deposit pattern. D: Sheetlike/multilaminar basement membrane deposits on confocal microscopy are a recognized EBMD deposit pattern (map-line equivalent). E: Confocal image showing numerous hyperreflective microdots, the dot component of EBMD; explicitly captioned in this EBMD patient. F: Patient confocal panel from the same EBMD examination showing Descemet folds and hyporeflective striae, but no vocabulary finding applies and the caption warns these...

(B) Hyporeflective lines (blue arrows) interspersed between highly reflective curvilinear changes in the basal epithelium (depth 46 µm). (C) Linear and ring-shaped highly reflective material in the epithelial basement membrane (depth 55 µm). (D) Sheetlike deposits in epithelial basement membrane (depth 63 µm). (E) Highly reflective microdots (blue arrows) spread in the anterior stroma (depth 82 µm). These findings may represent pressure-induced artifacts and should be distinguished from pathological changes.

panels.figure_caption: Image of the right eye of the proband in Family 2 (patient I-2). Slit-lamp (a), retroillumination (b), and fluorescein with vital stain (c) reveal multiple intraepithelial microcysts and map-dot–fingerprint dystrophy (white arrow). IVCM shows hyperreflective material and intraepithelial microcysts with well-defined edges in the epithelium (d); basal folds correspond to abnormal basement membrane deposits within basal epithelial cells (e,f) (IVCM images were acquired covering a 400 × 400 µm area, resulting in a lateral resolution of 1 µm/pixel).
in_text_mentions: I-3). Subepithelial scars were present in the proband and in the patient (II-1). In addition, the proband (I-2) and patient (II-1) revealed map-dot–fingerprint lesions as a manifestation of EBMD (see Figure 2). The affected child patient (III-1) exhibited diffuse epithelial punctate lesions without the presence of microcysts. The two unaffected patients, (II-2) and (III-2), had no visible corneal alterations. Dry eye tests were within normal values for all individuals, except for unaffected patient II-2, who had an altered Schirmer’s test (7mm OD and 5mm OS), probably related to his job as a c

ensity was 25 ± 2 (OD) and 34 ± 4 (OS) cysts/mm2, and the diameter ranged from 58.3 to 15.6 µm. Hyperreflective material, corresponding to cellular debris, was present both inside and outside the microcysts, with a density of 261 ± 14 cellular debris/mm2. Microcysts and hyperreflective material were located at depths between 3 µm and 55 µm. The images further showed an abnormal basement membrane with folds, Bowman’s membrane atrophy (compatible with EBMD), subepithelial nerve abnormalities, and active keratocytes with close keratocyte–nerve interaction in the stroma (see Table 2 and Figure 2).

IVCM shows hyperreflective material and intraepithelial microcysts with well-defined edges in the epithelium (d); basal folds correspond to abnormal basement membrane deposits within basal epithelial cells (e,f) (IVCM images were acquired covering a 400 × 400 µm area, resulting in a lateral resolution of 1 µm/pixel).
